policies.final_rule: source_attribution does not imply detection. Assign detection only when the paper explicitly performs an authenticity / real-versus-generated task. Classification among already-synthetic generators is attribution only.

localization requires an evaluated spatial forensic prediction task such as pixel-, mask-, patch-, region-, or equivalent spatial prediction of synthetic/generated/edited content. Artifact segmentation qualifies. Attention maps, saliency maps, explainability heatmaps, or visualization alone do not qualify.

Every public paper must remain connected to at least one core forensic task represented by the map: detection, source_attribution, or localization. If careful review establishes that none applies, the record requires scope review rather than an empty task set.

policy_source.interpretation: Use finalized T3 MODIFY_AND_ACCEPT, not the superseded permissive proposal. Lack of a supported core task triggers scope review. These evidence conclusions propose reversible exclusion; they neither create a new policy nor authorize a placeholder task. Human-study methodology alone is not an exclusion criterion.

scientific_protocol.research_question: How do AI-image disclosure labels and label errors influence opinions, factual-claim judgments and trust?
scientific_protocol.qualitative_study: Five focus groups, 18 participants; semi-structured discussions and thematic coding of label expectations and recognition experiences (sections 3.1–3.2, Appendix A).
scientific_protocol.input_images: Human-made and AI-generated images paired with true or false claims in simulated social posts. Realistic AI images are stimulus material; generated origin and label assignment are controlled experimental variables.
scientific_protocol.human_response_endpoint: Per-post yes/no factual-claim belief (Q1) and four-level confidence (Q2); supplementary aggregate perceptions of labels, mislabeling and trust. No computational image-origin predictor is evaluated.
scientific_protocol.experimental_class_space: Claim response is yes/no against true/false claim ground truth. Human/AI image origin is crossed with claim veracity, not the scored response class. Group is control, labeling or mislabeling; post-study Q4/Q5 responses are yes/no/unsure impressions.
scientific_protocol.ground_truth_and_protocol: Study 2 uses 1,354 valid respondents after excluding 51 of 1,405 completions, a 2 × 2 × 3 mixed design and 24 common posts (six in each image-origin × claim-veracity cell) plus two attention checks. Captions are adapted where needed, notably to construct AI-image/true-claim stimuli. Known claim veracity scores responses; origin and label correctness are assigned stimulus factors. See section 4.1, Tables 2–3, Figure 1 and Appendix B.5–B.7/Table 7.
scientific_protocol.metrics: Claim-judgment accuracy; d-prime = z(H) − z(FA), where H is true claims rated true and FA is false claims rated true; response bias c = −(z(H)+z(FA))/2. GLMM models claim accuracy; ANOVA analyzes claim sensitivity/bias (sections 4.1–4.2, Tables 4–5).
scientific_protocol.absence_boundary: No independently evaluated authenticity, generator/model identification or spatial forensic prediction is established in this version. This is a report of examined evidence, not a claim that humans or any discussed system could never perform those tasks.

quantitative_findings.locator: PDF p. 11, section 4.2, Figure 2a; statistical contrasts in Table 5
quantitative_findings.metric: Correct false-claim judgment for AI/false posts
quantitative_findings.interpretation: Accuracy concerns claim veracity; these are not image-origin classification rates.

quantitative_findings.metric: Mean claim sensitivity d-prime, pooled image conditions
quantitative_findings.interpretation: Sensitivity separates true and false factual claims, not human and AI images.

quantitative_findings.locator: PDF p. 13, Figure 3b; PDF p. 26, Appendix B.5 Q4/Q5
quantitative_findings.metric: Retrospective impression that unlabeled AI images occurred
quantitative_findings.interpretation: Aggregate perception responses; the correctly labeled group nevertheless reported errors. No per-image authenticity score is defined for these questions.

counterexample_checks.finding: Q4/Q5 are global retrospective impressions, not identified-image predictions with scored ground truth. Appendix A.5 recognition prompts ask about prior experiences; qualitative opinions are not a separate evaluated forensic task.

counterexample_checks.finding: These are background or candidate labeling mechanisms discussed in sections 2, 3 and 5. The manuscript does not evaluate their authenticity, attribution or localization outputs.

scientific_protocol.research_question: Can physically plausible rendered split defects improve industrial inspection when real defective stamping examples are scarce?
scientific_protocol.input_images: Captured and rendered HDR images of stamped metal components. Necking and splitting are grouped as split defects. Synthetic imagery supplies annotated training examples; Stable Diffusion and DFMGAN are augmentation comparators.
scientific_protocol.method: Finite-element geometry/strain and a forming-limit curve choose plausible defect sites; captured crack-displacement textures, surface reflectance/impurities and path-traced rendering produce synthetic training images (sections III–IV).
scientific_protocol.model_prediction_endpoint: YOLOv5, Faster R-CNN and DETR predict physical split-defect regions/bounding boxes and confidence. Figures 12–13 compare predicted boxes to defect ground truth.
scientific_protocol.experimental_class_space: Target is physical split defect (including neck defects), not image authenticity or generator identity. Numeric class IDs are not enumerated in the reviewed manuscript. Real/synthetic denotes training or test domain; generators denote augmentation methods.
scientific_protocol.ground_truth_and_protocol: 120 in-house defective Nakajima parts provide real HDR images. Ten real samples form a split-texture dictionary. Real defects have human annotations; generated masks supply synthetic defect labels, with label randomization. Section V reports 2,000 training epochs and five-fold cross-validation, retaining the same fold test sets across combinations. Table II varies real/synthetic training counts; Table III compares augmentation/pretraining; Table IV and Figures 12–13 check ablations and defect detections on real/synthetic test domains.
scientific_protocol.metrics: mAP50 and mAP averaged over IoU thresholds 0.50–0.95 in 0.05 increments, measured against defect-region annotations (section VI.A; Tables II–IV).
scientific_protocol.absence_boundary: No evaluated synthetic-origin, generating-model or manipulated-region provenance output is reported across the examined protocols. Physical defect boxes and synthesis masks are not forensic localization. This does not assert general incapability of the architectures.

quantitative_findings.locator: PDF p. 8 / article p. 7, Table II, YOLOv5, real=80 row
quantitative_findings.interpretation: Rows are real training counts; columns are synthetic counts. Improvement is in downstream industrial inspection.

quantitative_findings.interpretation: Generators provide alternative training data; they are not predicted source labels.

quantitative_findings.interpretation: Separate test domains for the defect task, not real-versus-synthetic classification.

counterexample_checks.finding: Section V.B/Figure 9 masks provide physical defect annotations. Figures 12–13 and section VI.C score physical cracks/splits; no synthetic/edit provenance target is evaluated.
